info.name: CafePOS — Phases 0–2
info.description:
Every endpoint the API exposes through Phase 2 (foundations, identity, catalog).

## Setup

1. `docker compose up -d && pnpm db:migrate && pnpm db:seed && pnpm start:dev`
2. Run **Auth → Login as ADMIN**. Its test script writes `accessToken` into a collection variable, and every other request inherits `Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}` from the collection. Nothing else needs a token pasted by hand.
3. Access tokens last 15 minutes. When requests start returning 401 `AUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED`, run a login again — or **Auth → Refresh**, which rotates the pair and re-captures both.

Logging in as MANAGER, CASHIER or BARISTA overwrites the same variable, so the whole collection re-runs as that role. That is the quickest way to exercise the §6.4 permission matrix by hand: sign in as BARISTA, then try `POST /categories` and watch it 403.

## Requests that capture variables

| Request | Sets |
|---|---|
| Auth → Login / Refresh | `accessToken`, `refreshToken` |
| Devices → Register a kiosk | `deviceId`, `pairingCode` |
| Devices → Activate | `deviceToken` |
| Menu → Get the menu | `menuEtag` |
| Categories / Items / Option groups → Create | `categoryId`, `itemId`, `optionGroupId`, `optionId` |

So the folders work top to bottom: create a category, and the item request already points at it.

## Conventions (DESIGN.md §5.1)

Money is integer minor units — `8500` is ฿85.00. Ids are UUIDv7. Errors are RFC 9457 problem documents; switch on `code`, never on `detail`. Every response carries `X-Request-Id`.

## Rate limits are real (§10.2)

20 logins per 15 min per address, **5 device activations per hour**, 600 requests/min per staff user. Five failed logins also lock that one account for 15 minutes. Clear them all with:

```
redis-cli --scan --pattern 'throttle:*' | xargs redis-cli del
```

item.name: Health
item.description: Both probes sit at the root, outside /api/v1, so orchestrators target paths that never move with an API version. Neither needs a token.

request.description: Checks no dependencies on purpose: a slow database must not get the container killed.
Pings Postgres and Redis with a 2s timeout each. 503 names the dependency that failed.

item.name: Auth
item.description: Four logins for the four roles. Each writes the same `accessToken` variable, so whichever you ran last is the identity the rest of the collection uses.

exec: console.log('Signed in as ADMIN; token expires in ' + body.expiresInSeconds + 's');

request.description: Run this first. Returns `accessToken` (15 min, HS256 JWT), `refreshToken` (14 days, opaque) and `expiresInSeconds`.
A manager can do everything in the catalog but cannot touch `/users`.
Reads the menu and flips availability. Everything else in the catalog is 403.
Sign in here, then try `Categories → Create` to watch the role matrix refuse it.

exec: console.log('Rotated. The previous refresh token is now dead.');

request.description:
Public, because the token *is* the credential.

Rotation retires the presented token. Send the same one twice and the second call revokes the entire token family — the standard stolen-token response (§6.1). Worth doing once deliberately: hit Send twice, then watch every later request 401 until you log in again.
The only endpoint both staff and kiosks may call. Returns `type: "staff"` with a role, or `type: "device"` — the shape a client uses to tell which kind of principal it is holding.
204. Revokes the session behind the presented access token.

item.name: Users
item.description: ADMIN-only except the list, which managers may read. Requires `Login as ADMIN`.

request.description:
Password minimum is 10 characters and nothing else — no character-class theater, which only pushes people toward `Password1!` (§6.1).

Emails are `citext`, so `A@x.com` collides with `a@x.com` on the unique index.
ADMIN and MANAGER. Password hashes are never in the response.

Any of `displayName`, `role`, `isActive` — at least one; an empty PATCH is a client bug and answers 400 rather than hiding it behind a 200.

Demoting or deactivating the last active admin is refused (`LAST_ADMIN`): try it on the seeded admin to see the guard fire.

item.name: Devices (kiosks)
item.description:
The pairing flow, in order: Register → Activate → the kiosk holds a token.

Only **5 activations per hour per address** (§10.2), so don't brute-force this folder.

exec: console.log('Pairing code ' + body.pairingCode + ' — shown once, only its hash is stored.');

request.description: Returns `pairingCode` **once** — the row keeps only its hash. The test script captures it, so Activate below already has it. Codes expire in 10 minutes (`PAIRING_CODE_TTL_SECONDS`).

item.name: Activate (exchange the code for a token)

exec: console.log('Device token captured — use "Get the menu (as a kiosk)".');

request.description:
Public — the code is the credential, since a tablet being set up holds nothing else yet.

Returns a 256-bit opaque `deviceToken`, not a JWT. It is a database row precisely so revoking a stolen tablet takes effect on the very next request (§6.2). Lower case and stray whitespace in the code are forgiven as transcription noise; a character outside the alphabet is not.
Status and last-seen per device. Token hashes are never returned.

`name` and/or `status` (`ACTIVE` | `PAUSED`). Retiring a tablet is deliberately *not* reachable here — that is the revoke route below.

With the device paused, re-run **Get the menu (as a kiosk)** and watch it refuse.
204, and the token is dead immediately — no waiting for an expiry. Its own route rather than a status field, because killing a tablet is a deliberate act, not an edit.

item.name: Menu (the kiosk read)
item.description: The one endpoint tuned for polling, and the only catalog route a device may call.

exec: console.log('ETag ' + etag + ' captured — try the 304 request next.');
console.log('No ETag: Redis is unreachable, so the menu was built straight from Postgres.');

request.description:
Categories → items → option groups → options in one document, and the only read a kiosk makes.

Carries `ETag: W/"catalog-<version>"` and `Cache-Control: private, no-cache`. `no-cache` rather than a `max-age` is deliberate: a client-side lifetime would stack on top of the poll interval and put the 10-second propagation budget (FR-3) out of reach.

Unlike the management `GET`s, this hides inactive categories and 86'd items — it is what the customer sees.

If Redis is down the menu still serves, built fresh from Postgres and without an ETag. The cache is a cache: a slower menu is a worse cafe, an erroring one is a closed cafe.

exec: console.log('304 — one Redis read, no database work. This is the kiosk polling every 10s.');

request.description:
Run **Get the menu** first to capture the ETag.

Expect 304. Then make any catalog write — 86 an item, rename a category — and run this again: the version counter has moved, so you get a fresh 200. Every write path moves it, via an interceptor on the write controllers rather than a call at the end of each service method.

Same endpoint, device token instead of a staff JWT — run the Devices folder first.

Both credential kinds arrive through `Authorization: Bearer` and are told apart by shape: a JWT is three dot-separated segments, a device token is one base64url word.

This is the *only* catalog route a device may call. Point the token at `/categories` or `/items` and the role matrix refuses it.

item.name: Categories
item.description: Management reads: these return inactive rows too, because a back office cannot restore what it cannot see.

request.description:
`sortOrder` and `isActive` are optional — the table defaults them to 0 and true, and a form that only knows the name should not have to invent the rest.

Names are unique; sending this twice answers 409.
Includes inactive categories, unlike `GET /menu`.
Any of `name`, `sortOrder`, `isActive`. Deactivating hides the whole category from `GET /menu` — a clean way to watch the ETag move.

item.name: Items
item.description: Run `Create a category` first, or set `categoryId` by hand to one from `GET /categories`.

request.description:
`basePriceMinor` is satang: 11000 is ฿110.00. Capped at 1,000,000 (฿10,000) — above that is a misplaced decimal, and catching it here beats finding it on a receipt.

`imageUrl` may be sent directly but must be **https** — the value is rendered as an image source by unattended tablets, and `z.url()` alone would accept `javascript:`.
Includes 86'd items, unlike `GET /menu`.

Name, price, photo, category — availability is deliberately absent, see the next request.

`description` and `imageUrl` are nullable here: `undefined` means leave it, `null` means clear it.

The one catalog write a CASHIER or BARISTA may make. Sign in as BARISTA and run this, then try `Update an item` — the split between the two routes is exactly what lets whoever is standing at the bar 86 the oat milk without also holding the rights to reprice it (FR-3).

PUT, not PATCH: the body is the *complete* set of groups this item offers, so sending it twice leaves the same rows. An empty array detaches everything.

Display order is the array's own order — a list cannot express a duplicate rank or a gap, so "two groups both claim position 3" stops being a case anyone has to rule on.

Run `Option groups → Create` first to fill `optionGroupId`.

**Pick a file in the Body tab before sending** — Postman cannot store one inside a collection.

The only multipart route in the API, and the only place it accepts bytes it did not author. Held in memory, never written to the API's filesystem, capped at 5 MB.

Nothing is stored as sent: the format is read from the file's own magic bytes rather than the `Content-Type` you choose, then decoded and re-encoded to WebP at a 1600px long edge. A polyglot file, an appended archive, or EXIF carrying the photographer's home GPS does not survive being re-rendered from pixels. SVG is refused outright — it is a document format that can carry script, and these images are served to unattended public tablets.

The response's `imageUrl` points at MinIO; the key is the SHA-256 of the *output*, so re-uploading the same photo yields the same key. Answers 200, not 201: the resource already existed.

item.name: Option groups & options
item.description: Groups are shared across items — one `Size` group, attached wherever it applies, rather than a copy per drink.

request.description: `minSelect` ≤ `maxSelect`, both 0–50. Omitted, they default to 0 and 1 — and the schema validates against those same defaults, so a create sending only one bound is judged against the value the row will actually get.
Groups with their options.

A PATCH moving only one bound is judged against the other as it stands in the database — which only the CHECK constraint can see, so an invalid pair surfaces as `OPTION_GROUP_MINMAX_INVALID` rather than a Zod error.

item.name: Add an option to a group

request.description:
`priceDeltaMinor` may be **negative** (±100,000) — the column carries no CHECK, unlike `base_price_minor`, because "small size, −10฿" is a real menu. The seeded `Size → Small` is −1000.

Keeping a line total off the floor is Phase 3's job: only server-side pricing sees the whole basket.
`name`, `priceDeltaMinor`, `isDefault`. Availability is absent for the same reason it is absent from the item update — it is separately authorized.
Any staff member, like the item toggle. This is the oat-milk case: the choice disappears from `GET /menu` while the drinks offering it stay on sale.
